overview: Only a handful of countries, mostly in Latin America and the Caribbean, still formally recognize Taiwan, and this bill makes it U.S. policy to support those countries and counter Chinese pressure on them to switch their recognition to Beijing. It directs the State Department to set up a system to track Chinese infrastructure and development projects in those countries, flag risky or non-transparent deals, and coordinate U.S. responses. The department must report to Congress twice a year on any governments moving to drop ties with Taiwan, provide a plan within 30 days to help keep those ties if one is, and issue annual reports for five years. It also requires briefings on U.S. help for Taiwan against Chinese influence campaigns and on deterrence in the Taiwan Strait. As of October 30, 2025, a Senate committee had approved it and it was placed on the Senate's calendar, meaning it is eligible for a vote by the full Senate.
for: Supporters say China has used opaque deals and pressure to peel away Taiwan's partners one by one, and a coordinated U.S. response would help those countries make their own choices.
against: Critics say the bill relies mostly on monitoring and reports, and actively lobbying other countries over whom they recognize could draw the U.S. deeper into a diplomatic contest with China.
